four.title: When You Set Boundaries, Why Do They Suddenly Call You 'Difficult'?
four.excerpt: Setting psychological boundaries isn't aggression or arrogance, it's a sign of a healthy sense of self. Here's why people around you react the way they do once you stop trying to please everyone.
four.author: Dr. Nader Attallah

content.value: Have you ever noticed that the moment you stop letting people take advantage of you, and start setting boundaries in draining relationships, some of them suddenly start calling you 'difficult' or say your temper has 'gotten harsh'? That reaction is usually not really about you, it's about their discomfort with a dynamic they had grown used to suddenly changing.
Why does setting boundaries upset people?

In psychology, this reaction has a name: Threatened Control. Someone who was used to you always being available, quiet, and accommodating genuinely feels anxious when you suddenly establish clear boundaries, because they've lost a form of control they had come to rely on.

People who benefited from your kindness may, once you set boundaries, try to 'punish' you socially, whether through negative talk, damaging your reputation, or even false accusations. All of these attempts share one goal: pulling you back into the old role they were comfortable with.
Their resentment reflects them, not you

In psychology, much of this hostile reaction is understood as a form of projection, where a person projects their own internal frustration onto you, as a reaction to losing a privilege they had come to see as a right, even though it was never truly a right to begin with, just something your kindness allowed.
Setting boundaries is a skill, not aggression

It's important to distinguish between setting boundaries and being aggressive. Setting boundaries is a core psychological skill that protects your energy, but just as important is learning to let go of the guilt that often follows the first time you actually enforce one.

Respecting yourself enough to set healthy boundaries isn't arrogance, it's a sign of a healthy sense of self. True inner peace never begins with pleasing everyone around you. It begins the moment you stop hurting yourself just to keep others comfortable.

five.title: Sleep and Mental Health: A Deeper Connection Than You Think
five.excerpt: Poor sleep isn't just physical fatigue, it's a direct factor in increased anxiety and mood swings. Discover the real relationship between your sleep and your mental health.
five.author: Dr. Sarah Ahmed

content.value: Many of us treat poor sleep as a minor inconvenience or temporary tiredness, but sleep is actually one of the most important factors shaping our day-to-day mental health. During sleep, the brain processes emotions and memories, and resets the chemical balance responsible for mood.
How poor sleep affects your mental state

When we repeatedly sleep less than our body needs, our tolerance for daily stress drops, and emotional reactions become more intense. This explains why, after a bad night's sleep, small things can bother us more than usual, or we feel anxious without a clear reason.
Signs your sleep is affecting your mental health

items: Difficulty concentrating even on simple tasks
Rapid mood swings without an obvious cause
Constant fatigue even after enough hours of sleep
A noticeable increase in anxiety or tension

content.value: Practical steps to improve your sleep quality

Sticking to a consistent sleep and wake schedule, even on weekends, helps your body build a stable internal rhythm. Avoiding screens for about an hour before bed and reducing evening caffeine intake are simple steps that make a real, noticeable difference over time.

If sleep problems persist despite healthy habits, it's worth consulting a specialist, since sleep disorders are sometimes a symptom of another underlying condition that needs proper evaluation and follow-up.

six.title: Mindfulness: A Simple Daily Tool to Calm the Mind
six.excerpt: Mindfulness isn't a passing trend, it's a scientifically supported practice for reducing stress and increasing present-moment awareness.
six.author: Dr. Mohamed Hassan

content.value: Mindfulness is simply the ability to be mentally present in the moment you're in, without getting caught up in constant thoughts about the past or worries about the future. The idea is simple, but practicing it takes training and consistency.
Why mindfulness matters for mental health

Much of our anxiety and stress comes from our minds constantly dwelling on future events that haven't happened yet, or replaying past situations. Practicing mindfulness helps quiet this excess mental activity, making it easier to notice your thoughts and feelings without being swept away by them.
Simple ways to practice mindfulness daily

items: Spend 5 minutes a day focusing only on your breathing
Notice small sensory details during an everyday activity like eating or walking
When your mind wanders, gently notice it and return your focus without self-judgment
Try writing down 3 things you noticed today, without evaluating them

content.value: The long-term result

Regular practice, even just a few minutes a day, gradually reduces the intensity of anxiety and improves your ability to handle stressful situations more calmly. The benefit doesn't show up immediately, but it builds over time with consistency, just like any other skill.

seven.title: Digital Balance: How to Protect Your Mental Health from Screen Overload
seven.excerpt: Excessive social media use is linked to increased feelings of comparison and anxiety. Here's how to build a healthier relationship with your screen.
seven.author: Lahazat Moments Team

content.value: Screens have become an essential part of our daily lives, but excessive use of social media in particular has been linked in numerous studies to increased anxiety, social comparison, and dissatisfaction with one's personal life.
Why does social media affect our mood?

We naturally tend to compare our everyday lives to the best moments others share online, creating an unrealistic gap between what we're actually living and what we see. Over time, this gap can affect self-esteem and increase feelings of anxiety or inadequacy.
Signs it's time to rethink your relationship with your screen

items: The first thing you do each morning is open social media
You feel anxious or uneasy after long browsing sessions
You frequently compare yourself to others
You miss out on real time with people around you because of your phone

content.value: Practical steps toward a healthier digital balance

Setting specific times of day for browsing instead of checking randomly and constantly, and unfollowing accounts that trigger negative comparison, are simple, practical first steps. Dedicating a screen-free time each day, even just thirty minutes, also helps your mind rest and naturally reset its focus.
